segments.text: Good morning, and welcome to the National eGovernance Summit 2026. Over the next two days we have more than forty speakers from central ministries, state governments and industry, and one simple question in front of us: how do we make digital public infrastructure work for every citizen, not just the connected ones?

Before I invite our chief guest, a word on format. Every session today is being recorded, and the eGov team will be publishing a special issue from these discussions. So speak freely, but speak on the record.

Thank you, Anil. Ten years ago we were debating whether citizens would trust a digital identity. Today the debate is very different. The rails are built. The question now is what we run on them, and who gets left behind when we do.

Let me share one number that I think about every week. In the last financial year, our citizen services platform handled 1.4 billion transactions. But nearly 30 percent of those were assisted, meaning someone at a service centre did it on behalf of the citizen.

That is not a failure. That is a design input. Assisted digital is how inclusion actually happens in this country, and our next generation of platforms must treat the service centre operator as a first-class user.

We are announcing today that the department will publish open interface standards for assisted service delivery by March 2027, so that every state can plug its own service centres into a common grievance and tracking layer.

Infrastructure is only public when every citizen can actually use it. If a widow in a district headquarters cannot get her pension certificate without three visits, then our infrastructure is not finished, however elegant the architecture diagrams look.

From the state side, I want to add a practical lens. We moved 212 services online in the last three years. The ones that succeeded had one thing in common: we redesigned the process before we digitised it.
The ones that struggled were the ones where we simply converted a paper form into a web form. Citizens could tell the difference immediately.

Our average time to deliver a caste or income certificate came down from 21 days to 4 days. But the bigger change was predictability. Citizens now get an SMS with a committed date, and we hold ourselves to it.

Data sharing between departments is the next frontier, and it has to be consent-based. Citizens must be able to see which department accessed their records and why. Trust is not a slogan; it is an audit log the citizen can read.
Questions from the floor. Yes, the gentleman in the third row.

The question is about funding for smaller states. Honestly, the constraint is less about money and more about people. We will be running a shared capacity programme with twelve states to place product managers inside departments.
And if I may add, the best investment we made was training our own district officers. Technology vendors come and go. Institutional capability stays.
Thank you both. That sets the tone for everything that follows.
Welcome to our panel on AI for governance. Everyone has run a pilot. Very few have run a platform. So let us talk about what it takes to cross that gap.

The honest answer is that most pilots fail on data, not on models. We found that in nine out of eleven pilots we reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began.
So the programme office is now funding data readiness first. Before a department gets money for an AI model, it has to show us a data inventory and a named data steward.
From the industry side, I would add that procurement is still designed for buying hardware. AI systems need to be evaluated continuously after deployment, and our contracts rarely allow for that.

We worked with one state on grievance classification. The model was 91 percent accurate in testing. In the first month of production it dropped to 78 percent because citizens wrote complaints very differently from the training data.
That is exactly why human review has to stay in the loop for anything that affects entitlements. AI can sort and route, but a person must decide when someone's benefit is at stake.
Farah, is there a framework coming that departments can actually follow?

Yes. We will release a risk-tiered AI deployment framework for public services in the first quarter of next year. Low-risk uses like document summarisation get a fast track. High-risk uses like eligibility decisions need an impact assessment and an appeal mechanism.

Language is the other big opportunity. Voice interfaces in local languages can do more for inclusion than any app redesign. A farmer should be able to ask about a scheme in her own dialect and get an accurate answer.
But accuracy in local languages is uneven. We should publish evaluation benchmarks by language so that departments know where a system is reliable and where it is not.
A question from the audience on job losses in government offices.
Our experience is that AI changes the work rather than removing it. Clerks who spent days on data entry now spend that time on verification and citizen follow-up.
Build small, measure honestly, and scale only what works. That is the whole playbook.
On that note, thank you to our panel.
Cyber resilience is no longer an IT problem. When a hospital system or a land records portal goes down, it is a governance failure that citizens feel immediately.
Last year our coordination centre handled 2,300 reported incidents across state departments. Most were phishing and credential misuse, not sophisticated attacks.
Which tells you where the investment should go. Identity, access management and basic hygiene will prevent more damage than the most advanced threat intelligence platform.
I would push the room on recovery. Every department has a backup policy. Very few have tested a full restore in the last twelve months.
We are making that mandatory. From next April, critical state systems must complete and document a restore drill twice a year.
Supply chain is the other blind spot. Your security is only as strong as the smallest vendor with access to your network.
Resilience means assuming you will be breached and designing so that the citizen service keeps running anyway.
We also need more security professionals in government. Our centre is creating a cadre of 150 trained officers who will sit inside departments rather than in a central team.
And please, share incidents. The department that hides an attack helps the attacker hit the next department.
Thank you. Let us keep this conversation going beyond the summit.
Kirti, cities have been collecting data for a decade now. What has actually changed for residents?
The biggest change is that we stopped building dashboards for officials and started building services for residents. A dashboard does not fix a pothole.
Our integrated command centre now routes civic complaints directly to field teams. The average time to close a water supply complaint fell from six days to under two.
What made that possible? Technology or process?
Process first. We gave ward engineers a single mobile app and made closure photographs mandatory. Accountability became visible.
There is a risk that smart city projects become vendor showcases. How do you avoid that?
We insist on open data standards in every contract. If we cannot take our data and move to another vendor, we do not sign.
The next step is predictive maintenance. We have sensors on 340 pumping stations, and we want to fix failures before residents notice them.
Final question: what should a smaller city do first?
Start with one service residents complain about the most, fix it end to end, and publish the results. Trust compounds.
Interoperability is the word everyone uses and very few define. For us it means a patient's record follows the patient, with consent, across public and private facilities.
In our state, 4.2 crore health IDs have been created, but creation is the easy part. The harder metric is how many records are actually linked to those IDs. Today that number is around 38 percent.
The private sector is ready to integrate, but we need stable APIs and clear certification. Every time a specification changes without notice, smaller clinics drop off.
We have heard that feedback. From January, our state sandbox will offer a certification track with fixed release windows twice a year.
Data quality is the silent problem. If a diagnosis is entered as free text in three different spellings, no analytics system will save you.
Telemedicine showed what is possible. In remote blocks, teleconsultations now account for a fifth of all outpatient visits at primary health centres.
Consent must be meaningful. We are testing a voice-based consent flow for patients who cannot read the screen.
Privacy and utility are not opposites. Good architecture gives you both.
The goal is simple: no patient should have to carry a plastic bag of old prescriptions to a new doctor.
Thank you all.
Every state is now a data organisation, whether it likes it or not. The question is where that data lives and who controls it.
Our state data centre has migrated 64 departmental applications to a government community cloud over the last two years.
Migration is not about moving servers. It is about retiring old applications that nobody remembers how to maintain.
From the provider side, sovereign cloud means three things: data residency, operational control by cleared personnel, and the ability to exit without penalty.
We are adopting a cloud-first policy for all new state applications from the next financial year, with a clear exception process for systems that must remain on-premise.
Cost visibility is essential. Departments should see what they consume every month, otherwise cloud bills become the new legacy problem.
Thank you, and I look forward to the discussions.
Agri-stack is about putting the farmer at the centre of the data, not the scheme.
We have digitised land records for 96 percent of villages in the state. The next step is linking them to crop surveys done by field staff using a mobile app.
For farmers, the value shows up when a loan or an insurance claim gets processed without a middleman. That is the test.
Connectivity is still the bottleneck. In some blocks, field staff upload survey data at the end of the day from the one spot with a signal.
Offline-first apps were the single biggest improvement we made. Data syncs whenever the network returns.
Advisory services in local languages are where AI can help, but the advice must be accountable to an agronomist.
Our common service centres processed crop insurance enrolments for farmers who had never used a smartphone. The village entrepreneur is the bridge.
Women farmers are under-represented in land records. Inclusion has to be measured, not assumed.
Thank you.
Good evening and welcome to the eGovernance Excellence Awards 2026. This year the jury reviewed 286 nominations from 27 states and union territories.
The jury looked for three things: measurable citizen impact, the ability to scale, and honesty about what did not work.
Several entries this year came from district administrations, which tells us innovation is no longer only a capital-city story.
Recognition matters because it gives officers permission to take risks. Most good ideas in government die because nobody wants to be the first to try.
The award for Citizen Service Delivery goes to a district team that cut pension processing time from forty-five days to seven.
To every officer here: document what you did, so that someone in another state can copy it next year.
Thank you for joining us, and we will see you at the next summit.

articles.subheadline: Over two days in New Delhi, the National eGovernance Summit 2026 moved the conversation from launching platforms to making them work for everyone
articles.intro: More than forty speakers from ministries, state governments and industry gathered for the National eGovernance Summit 2026 with a deceptively simple question on the table: how do we make digital public infrastructure work for every citizen, not just the connected ones?

body.text: Opening the summit, Summit Chair Anil Varma set the tone with an unusual ground rule. Every session was being recorded for this special issue, he told delegates, so they should speak freely, but speak on the record. What followed over two days was a candid stock-take of what has worked, what has not, and what must change.

The inaugural address by Dr. Meera Raghavan, Secretary, Department of Digital Services, framed the agenda. The rails are built, she said; the question now is what runs on them, and who gets left behind. Her department will publish open interface standards for assisted service delivery by March 2027, allowing every state to connect its service centres to a common grievance and tracking layer.
Infrastructure is only public when every citizen can actually use it.
From pilots to platforms

The AI track was notably sober. Dr. Farah Siddiqui, Director of the National AI Programme Office, said that in nine out of eleven pilots her office reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began. Funding will now go to data readiness first, and a risk-tiered deployment framework for public services is due in the first quarter of next year.

Industry voices pressed for procurement reform. Prakash Nair, CTO of Kaveri Systems, described a grievance-classification model that was 91 percent accurate in testing but dropped to 78 percent in its first month of production, because citizens wrote complaints very differently from the training data.
Resilience, cities and health

On cyber security, the State Cyber Coordination Centre reported handling 2,300 incidents last year, most of them phishing and credential misuse. Critical state systems will have to complete and document a restore drill twice a year from next April.

In a fireside conversation on smart cities, Kirti Malhotra described routing civic complaints straight to field teams, cutting the average time to close a water-supply complaint from six days to under two. The health panel, meanwhile, separated the easy metric of health IDs created from the harder one of records actually linked to them.

The summit closed with the eGovernance Excellence Awards, where the jury reviewed 286 nominations from 27 states and union territories. If there was one thread connecting the two days, it was the jury chair's observation that innovation is no longer only a capital-city story.

articles.headline: Assume Breach, Keep Serving
articles.subheadline: Why cyber resilience is now a governance problem, and what states are doing about it
articles.intro: When a hospital system or a land-records portal goes down, citizens feel it immediately. The summit's cyber panel argued that resilience must be designed into public services, not bolted on.

body.text: Ashok Rao, Director General of the State Cyber Coordination Centre, opened by reframing the subject. Cyber resilience is no longer an IT problem, he said; an outage of a critical citizen system is a governance failure.

The coordination centre handled 2,500 reported incidents across state departments last year. Most were phishing and credential misuse rather than sophisticated attacks, which, as Sahyadri Data Systems CISO Nandini Joshi observed, tells departments exactly where to invest: identity, access management and basic hygiene.
Restore drills become mandatory

Imran Shaikh of Trident Secure pushed the room on recovery. Every department has a backup policy, he said, but very few have tested a full restore in the last twelve months. Rao responded with an announcement: from next April, critical state systems must complete and document a restore drill twice a year.
Resilience means assuming you will be breached and designing so that the citizen service keeps running anyway.
Joshi flagged the supply chain as the other blind spot: a department's security is only as strong as the smallest vendor with access to its network.
People inside departments
Rao said the centre is creating a cadre of 150 trained officers who will sit inside departments rather than in a central team. Joshi closed with a plea for openness.
The department that hides an attack helps the attacker hit the next department.

articles.headline: “Before a Department Gets Money for an AI Model, It Has to Show Us Its Data”
articles.subheadline: Dr. Farah Siddiqui, Director, National AI Programme Office, in conversation on the summit floor
articles.intro: Edited from her remarks on the AI for Governance panel, the programme director explains why her office now funds data readiness first, and what the forthcoming risk-tiered framework will mean for departments.

body.text: Most AI pilots in government do not scale. Why?

The honest answer is that most pilots fail on data, not on models. We found that in nine out of eleven pilots we reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began.
How has that changed the way your office funds projects?
The programme office is now funding data readiness first. Before a department gets money for an AI model, it has to show us a data inventory and a named data steward.
Departments say they lack clear rules. Is a framework coming?

Yes. We will release a risk-tiered AI deployment framework for public services in the first quarter of next year. Low-risk uses like document summarisation get a fast track. High-risk uses like eligibility decisions need an impact assessment and an appeal mechanism.
There is anxiety about jobs in government offices. What have you seen?
Our experience is that AI changes the work rather than removing it. Clerks who spent days on data entry now spend that time on verification and citizen follow-up.

articles.subheadline: S. Balasubramanian on community cloud, retiring legacy systems and a cloud-first policy
articles.intro: Every state is now a data organisation, whether it likes it or not, the Principal Secretary for IT & Electronics told the summit. The question is where that data lives and who controls it.

body.text: Over the last two years, the state data centre has migrated 64 departmental applications to a government community cloud. Migration, S. Balasubramanian stressed, is not about moving servers; it is about retiring old applications that nobody remembers how to maintain.
The state will adopt a cloud-first policy for all new applications from the next financial year, with a clear exception process for systems that must remain on-premise.
sovereign cloud means three things: data residency, operational control by cleared personnel, and the ability to exit without penalty.

Deepa Thomas, Head of Public Sector at Northwind Cloud India, added that cost visibility is essential. Departments should see what they consume every month, she said, otherwise cloud bills become the new legacy problem.

articles.headline: A Dashboard Does Not Fix a Pothole
articles.subheadline: How one city company turned its command centre from a display wall into a service engine
articles.intro: Cities have collected data for a decade. In a fireside conversation, Kirti Malhotra, CEO of City Smart Services Company, explained what has actually changed for residents.

body.text: The biggest change, Malhotra told Rohan Mehta of Urban Futures Advisory, is that the city stopped building dashboards for officials and started building services for residents.
A dashboard does not fix a pothole.
The integrated command centre now routes civic complaints directly to field teams. The average time to close a water-supply complaint fell from six days to under two.
Process before technology

Asked whether technology or process made the difference, she was unequivocal: process first. Ward engineers were given a single mobile app and closure photographs were made mandatory. Accountability, she said, became visible.
Mehta raised the risk that smart-city projects become vendor showcases. Malhotra's answer was contractual: open data standards in every contract.
If we cannot take our data and move to another vendor, we do not sign.
Fixing failures before residents notice
The next step is predictive maintenance. The city has sensors on 340 pumping stations and wants to fix failures before residents notice them.
Her advice to smaller cities was simple: start with the one service residents complain about most, fix it end to end, and publish the results. Trust compounds.

articles.headline: The Record Should Follow the Patient
articles.subheadline: Health IDs are the easy part. Linking records, certifying APIs and earning consent are not
articles.intro: Interoperability is the word everyone uses and very few define, said Dr. Arvind Kulkarni of the Institute of Health Systems. For his panel, it meant one thing: a patient's record follows the patient, with consent, across public and private facilities.

body.text: Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh, CEO of the State Health Digital Mission, drew a sharp line between two metrics. In her state, 4.2 crore health IDs have been created, but creation is the easy part. The harder measure is how many records are actually linked to those IDs — today that number is around 38 percent.
Stable APIs for small clinics

Pooja Agarwal of Medisync Technologies said the private sector is ready to integrate but needs stable APIs and clear certification. Every unannounced specification change, she said, causes smaller clinics to drop off.
Dr. Venkatesh responded that from January the state sandbox will offer a certification track with fixed release windows twice a year.
Privacy and utility are not opposites. Good architecture gives you both.
Quality and consent

Dr. Kulkarni called data quality the silent problem: if a diagnosis is entered as free text in three different spellings, no analytics system will save you. Agarwal pointed to telemedicine as proof of what is possible — in remote blocks, teleconsultations now account for a fifth of all outpatient visits at primary health centres.
Consent, the panel agreed, must be meaningful. The state is testing a voice-based consent flow for patients who cannot read the screen.
No patient should have to carry a plastic bag of old prescriptions to a new doctor.

articles.headline: Putting the Farmer at the Centre of the Data
articles.subheadline: Land records, offline-first apps and village entrepreneurs are making agri-stack real — but inclusion has to be measured
articles.intro: Agri-stack is about putting the farmer at the centre of the data, not the scheme, said Manish Dubey of the Common Services Network, opening a panel that kept returning to the realities of the last mile.

body.text: Gurpreet Sandhu, Commissioner for Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, reported that land records have been digitised for 96 percent of villages in the state. The next step is linking them to crop surveys conducted by field staff on a mobile app.
For farmers, the value shows up when a loan or an insurance claim gets processed without a middleman.

Dr. Sneha Patil, founder of KisanGrid, said that is the real test of the stack. Advisory services in local languages are where AI can help, she added, but the advice must be accountable to an agronomist.
Designing for no signal

Connectivity remains the bottleneck. Aparna Iyengar of the Rural Connectivity Foundation described field staff in some blocks uploading survey data at the end of the day from the one spot with a signal. Sandhu said offline-first apps were the single biggest improvement the state made: data syncs whenever the network returns.
Dubey credited common service centres for processing crop-insurance enrolments for farmers who had never used a smartphone. The village entrepreneur, he said, is the bridge.
Iyengar closed with a pointed reminder that women farmers are under-represented in land records.
Inclusion has to be measured, not assumed.

articles.headline: What “AI-Ready Data” Actually Means for Government
articles.subheadline: Data inventories, named stewards and language benchmarks: the unglamorous groundwork behind every successful model
articles.intro: Across the summit's AI, health and cyber sessions, speakers kept arriving at the same conclusion from different directions: the model is rarely the hard part.

body.text: The National AI Programme Office now asks departments for two things before it funds a model: a data inventory and a named data steward. The requirement follows its review of pilots, in which nine out of eleven departments lacked a clean, labelled dataset at the outset.
Drift is the default

A model that performs well in testing can degrade quickly in production. Kaveri Systems described a grievance classifier that fell from 91 percent accuracy in testing to 78 percent in its first month live, because real complaints were written differently from the training data. Continuous evaluation, the panel argued, must be written into contracts.

Health systems face the same issue at the point of entry. If a diagnosis is entered as free text in three different spellings, no analytics system will save you, Dr. Arvind Kulkarni told the digital health panel.
Benchmarks by language

Voice interfaces in local languages were widely seen as the largest inclusion opportunity. But accuracy is uneven, and panellists called for evaluation benchmarks to be published by language so departments know where a system is reliable and where it is not.
A practical checklist
A data inventory and a named steward before model funding.
Contracts that pay for evaluation after deployment, not only delivery.
Human review for any decision that affects entitlements.
Published accuracy benchmarks for each supported language.

articles.headline: Redesign First, Digitise Second
articles.subheadline: Sunita Deshmukh on moving 212 services online — and why some of them struggled
articles.intro: A state mission director's account of what separates digital services citizens trust from those they merely tolerate.

body.text: Sunita Deshmukh's state moved 212 services online in the last three years. The ones that succeeded, the Mission Director told the inaugural session, had one thing in common: the process was redesigned before it was digitised. The ones that struggled were those where a paper form was simply converted into a web form — and citizens could tell the difference immediately.

The results show up in delivery times. The average time to deliver a caste or income certificate came down from 21 days to 4 days. But the bigger change, she said, was predictability: citizens now receive an SMS with a committed date, and the department holds itself to it.
we redesigned the process before we digitised it.
Her advice on capability was equally direct. The best investment the state made was training its own district officers. Technology vendors come and go, she said; institutional capability stays.

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
^ Two days at the National eGovernance Summit left one idea ringing louder than any product launch: the rails are built, and the work now is to make sure nobody is left on the platform.

When the Secretary for Digital Services told a packed hall that nearly 30 percent of transactions on a national citizen platform are completed with help from a service-centre operator, there was a brief silence. In many conference rooms that figure would be presented as a problem to be engineered away. Here it was presented as a design brief.

That shift in framing ran through the summit. A state mission director credited process redesign, not software, for cutting certificate delivery times. An AI programme director admitted that most pilots had failed for lack of clean data. A city chief executive reminded us that a dashboard does not fix a pothole.

This issue is our record of those conversations. Every quotation in these pages is linked to the recording in which it was spoken, and every figure has been checked against the session it came from. We think that discipline matters more than ever when the subject is public trust.

Read on for the keynotes, the panels and the people who are quietly rebuilding how government works. And if your department has done something worth copying, write to us. As one jury member put it on the final evening, innovation is no longer only a capital-city story.

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Building the Rails for a Digital Bharat

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Over two days in New Delhi, the National eGovernance Summit 2026 moved the conversation from launching platforms to making them work for everyone

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ More than forty speakers from ministries, state governments and industry gathered for the National eGovernance Summit 2026 with a deceptively simple question on the table: how do we make digital public infrastructure work for every citizen, not just the connected ones?

Opening the summit, Summit Chair Anil Varma set the tone with an unusual ground rule. Every session was being recorded for this special issue, he told delegates, so they should speak freely, but speak on the record. What followed over two days was a candid stock-take of what has worked, what has not, and what must change.

The inaugural address by Dr. Meera Raghavan, Secretary, Department of Digital Services, framed the agenda. The rails are built, she said; the question now is what runs on them, and who gets left behind. Her department will publish open interface standards for assisted service delivery by March 2027, allowing every state to connect its service centres to a common grievance and tracking layer.

## From pilots to platforms

The AI track was notably sober. Dr.

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“Infrastructure is only public when every citizen can actually use it.”

— Dr. Meera Raghavan

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
Farah Siddiqui, Director of the National AI Programme Office, said that in nine out of eleven pilots her office reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began. Funding will now go to data readiness first, and a risk-tiered deployment framework for public services is due in the first quarter of next year.

Industry voices pressed for procurement reform. Prakash Nair, CTO of Kaveri Systems, described a grievance-classification model that was 91 percent accurate in testing but dropped to 78 percent in its first month of production, because citizens wrote complaints very differently from the training data.

## Resilience, cities and health

On cyber security, the State Cyber Coordination Centre reported handling 2,300 incidents last year, most of them phishing and credential misuse. Critical state systems will have to complete and document a restore drill twice a year from next April.

In a fireside conversation on smart cities, Kirti Malhotra described routing civic complaints straight to field teams, cutting the average time to close a water-supply complaint from six days to under two. The health panel, meanwhile, separated the easy metric of health IDs created from the harder one of records actually linked to them.

The summit closed with the eGovernance Excellence Awards, where the jury reviewed 286 nominations from 27 states and union territories. If there was one thread connecting the two days, it was the jury chair's observation that innovation is no longer only a capital-city story.

elements.text: Keynote

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: “The Rails Are Built. Now We Must Ask Who Gets Left Behind”

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Dr. Meera Raghavan on why assisted digital delivery is a design input, not a failure

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Body text
elements.text:
^ In the summit's inaugural address, the Secretary for Digital Services argued that the next decade of digital public infrastructure will be measured by the citizens who still need help to use it.

Ten years ago, Dr. Meera Raghavan reminded the audience, the debate was whether citizens would trust a digital identity at all. That debate is over. The rails are built, she said, and the question has become what runs on them and who gets left behind when it does.

She offered one number she says she thinks about every week. In the last financial year, the citizen services platform handled 1.4 billion transactions, but nearly 30 percent of those were assisted, meaning someone at a service centre completed the transaction on the citizen's behalf.

Assisted digital, in her account, is how inclusion actually happens. The next generation of platforms must therefore treat the service-centre operator as a first-class user, with interfaces, training and accountability designed around them.

## Standards for assisted delivery

The address carried the summit's first concrete announcement. The department will publish open interface standards for assisted service delivery by March 2027, so that every state can plug its own service centres into a common grievance and tracking layer.

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: The inaugural session in progress

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“That is not a failure. That is a design input.”

— Dr. Meera Raghavan

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
The test of success, she said, is not architecture. If a widow in a district headquarters cannot get her pension certificate without three visits, the infrastructure is not finished, however elegant the diagrams look.

## Consent as the next frontier

Data sharing between departments is the next frontier, and it must be consent-based. Citizens should be able to see which department accessed their records and why — a principle she summarised in a line that drew sustained applause.

> “Trust is not a slogan; it is an audit log the citizen can read.” — Dr. Meera Raghavan

Asked from the floor about funding for smaller states, she said the constraint is less about money than about people. The department will run a shared capacity programme with twelve states to place product managers inside departments.

Sunita Deshmukh, Mission Director of the State e-Governance Mission, added the view from the field. Her state moved 212 services online in three years, and the successes shared one trait: the process was redesigned before it was digitised. Average delivery time for a caste or income certificate fell from 21 days to 4 days.

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Panel Discussion · AI for Governance

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Everyone Has Run a Pilot. Very Few Have Run a Platform

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Policymakers and technologists on the data, procurement and oversight it takes to scale AI in public services

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Vikram Sethi

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Moderating the summit's AI panel, eGov's Vikram Sethi opened with a provocation: everyone has run a pilot, very few have run a platform. The hour that followed was about crossing that gap.

Dr. Farah Siddiqui, Director of the National AI Programme Office, began with an uncomfortable finding. Most pilots fail on data, not on models: in nine out of eleven pilots her office reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began.

The programme office has changed its funding rules accordingly. Before a department receives money for an AI model, it must now show a data inventory and a named data steward.

## Contracts built for hardware

Prakash Nair, Chief Technology Officer at Kaveri Systems, said procurement is still designed for buying hardware, while AI systems need continuous evaluation after deployment. He described a grievance-classification model that was 91 percent accurate in testing and dropped to 78 percent in its first month of production, because citizens wrote complaints very differently from the training data.

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Dr. Farah Siddiqui on data readiness

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“AI can sort and route, but a person must decide when someone's benefit is at stake.”

— Harpreet Gill

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
Harpreet Gill of Northwind Cloud India argued that this is exactly why human review must stay in the loop for anything that affects entitlements.

## A risk-tiered framework

Asked whether departments would get a framework they can actually follow, Dr. Siddiqui confirmed that a risk-tiered AI deployment framework for public services will be released in the first quarter of next year. Low-risk uses such as document summarisation will get a fast track; high-risk uses such as eligibility decisions will need an impact assessment and an appeal mechanism.

Language emerged as the biggest opportunity and the biggest risk. Voice interfaces in local languages could do more for inclusion than any app redesign, Gill said. Nair cautioned that accuracy is uneven across languages and called for evaluation benchmarks to be published by language.

On jobs, Dr. Siddiqui said the programme's experience is that AI changes the work rather than removing it: clerks who spent days on data entry now spend that time on verification and citizen follow-up.

> “Build small, measure honestly, and scale only what works.” — Harpreet Gill

elements.text: Dr. Farah Siddiqui, Director, National AI Programme Office

^ Edited from her remarks on the AI for Governance panel, the programme director explains why her office now funds data readiness first, and what the forthcoming risk-tiered framework will mean for departments.

Q: Most AI pilots in government do not scale. Why?

The honest answer is that most pilots fail on data, not on models. We found that in nine out of eleven pilots we reviewed, the department did not have a clean, labelled dataset when the project began.

Q: How has that changed the way your office funds projects?

The programme office is now funding data readiness first. Before a department gets money for an AI model, it has to show us a data inventory and a named data steward.

Q: Departments say they lack clear rules. Is a framework coming?

Yes. We will release a risk-tiered AI deployment framework for public services in the first quarter of next year. Low-risk uses like document summarisation get a fast track. High-risk uses like eligibility decisions need an impact assessment and an appeal mechanism.

Q: There is anxiety about jobs in government offices. What have you seen?

Our experience is that AI changes the work rather than removing it. Clerks who spent days on data entry now spend that time on verification and citizen follow-up.

elements.text: Panel Discussion · Cyber Resilience

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Assume Breach, Keep Serving

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Why cyber resilience is now a governance problem, and what states are doing about it

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Ashok Rao, Director General, State Cyber Coordination Centre

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“Resilience means assuming you will be breached and designing so that the citizen service keeps running anyway.”

— Imran Shaikh

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ When a hospital system or a land-records portal goes down, citizens feel it immediately. The summit's cyber panel argued that resilience must be designed into public services, not bolted on.

Ashok Rao, Director General of the State Cyber Coordination Centre, opened by reframing the subject. Cyber resilience is no longer an IT problem, he said; an outage of a critical citizen system is a governance failure.

The coordination centre handled 2,500 reported incidents across state departments last year. Most were phishing and credential misuse rather than sophisticated attacks, which, as Sahyadri Data Systems CISO Nandini Joshi observed, tells departments exactly where to invest: identity, access management and basic hygiene.

## Restore drills become mandatory

Imran Shaikh of Trident Secure pushed the room on recovery. Every department has a backup policy, he said, but very few have tested a full restore in the last twelve months. Rao responded with an announcement: from next April, critical state systems must complete and document a restore drill twice a year.

Joshi flagged the supply chain as the other blind spot: a department's security is only as strong as the smallest vendor with access to its network.

## People inside departments

Rao said the centre is creating a cadre of 150 trained officers who will sit inside departments rather than in a central team. Joshi closed with a plea for openness.

> “The department that hides an attack helps the attacker hit the next department.” — Nandini Joshi

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Government Perspective

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Every State Is Now a Data Organisation

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: S. Balasubramanian on community cloud, retiring legacy systems and a cloud-first policy

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: S. Balasubramanian, Principal Secretary, IT & Electronics

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
^ Every state is now a data organisation, whether it likes it or not, the Principal Secretary for IT & Electronics told the summit. The question is where that data lives and who controls it.

Over the last two years, the state data centre has migrated 64 departmental applications to a government community cloud. Migration, S. Balasubramanian stressed, is not about moving servers; it is about retiring old applications that nobody remembers how to maintain.

The state will adopt a cloud-first policy for all new applications from the next financial year, with a clear exception process for systems that must remain on-premise.

Deepa Thomas, Head of Public Sector at Northwind Cloud India, added that cost visibility is essential. Departments should see what they consume every month, she said, otherwise cloud bills become the new legacy problem.

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“sovereign cloud means three things: data residency, operational control by cleared personnel, and the ability to exit without penalty.”

— Deepa Thomas

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Smart Cities

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: A Dashboard Does Not Fix a Pothole

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: How one city company turned its command centre from a display wall into a service engine

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Kirti Malhotra in conversation with Rohan Mehta

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Cities have collected data for a decade. In a fireside conversation, Kirti Malhotra, CEO of City Smart Services Company, explained what has actually changed for residents.

The biggest change, Malhotra told Rohan Mehta of Urban Futures Advisory, is that the city stopped building dashboards for officials and started building services for residents.

> “A dashboard does not fix a pothole.” — Kirti Malhotra

The integrated command centre now routes civic complaints directly to field teams. The average time to close a water-supply complaint fell from six days to under two.

## Process before technology

Asked whether technology or process made the difference, she was unequivocal: process first. Ward engineers were given a single mobile app and closure photographs were made mandatory. Accountability, she said, became visible.

Mehta raised the risk that smart-city projects become vendor showcases. Malhotra's answer was contractual: open data standards in every contract.

> “If we cannot take our data and move to another vendor, we do not sign.” — Kirti Malhotra

## Fixing failures before residents notice

The next step is predictive maintenance. The city has sensors on 340 pumping stations and wants to fix failures before residents notice them.

Her advice to smaller cities was simple: start with the one service residents complain about most, fix it end to end, and publish the results. Trust compounds.

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Panel Discussion · Digital Health

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: The Record Should Follow the Patient

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Health IDs are the easy part. Linking records, certifying APIs and earning consent are not

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Vikram Sethi

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh, CEO, State Health Digital Mission

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“Privacy and utility are not opposites. Good architecture gives you both.”

— Dr. Arvind Kulkarni

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Interoperability is the word everyone uses and very few define, said Dr. Arvind Kulkarni of the Institute of Health Systems. For his panel, it meant one thing: a patient's record follows the patient, with consent, across public and private facilities.

Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh, CEO of the State Health Digital Mission, drew a sharp line between two metrics. In her state, 4.2 crore health IDs have been created, but creation is the easy part. The harder measure is how many records are actually linked to those IDs — today that number is around 38 percent.

## Stable APIs for small clinics

Pooja Agarwal of Medisync Technologies said the private sector is ready to integrate but needs stable APIs and clear certification. Every unannounced specification change, she said, causes smaller clinics to drop off.

Dr. Venkatesh responded that from January the state sandbox will offer a certification track with fixed release windows twice a year.

## Quality and consent

Dr. Kulkarni called data quality the silent problem: if a diagnosis is entered as free text in three different spellings, no analytics system will save you. Agarwal pointed to telemedicine as proof of what is possible — in remote blocks, teleconsultations now account for a fifth of all outpatient visits at primary health centres.

Consent, the panel agreed, must be meaningful. The state is testing a voice-based consent flow for patients who cannot read the screen.

> “No patient should have to carry a plastic bag of old prescriptions to a new doctor.” — Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh

elements.text: “Consent Must Be Meaningful”

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh, CEO, State Health Digital Mission

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Vikram Sethi

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Dr. Lakshmi Venkatesh

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Edited from her panel remarks, the mission CEO on linking records, certifying private providers and designing consent for patients who cannot read a screen.

Q: Your state has created millions of health IDs. Is that the right measure of progress?

In our state, 4.2 crore health IDs have been created, but creation is the easy part. The harder metric is how many records are actually linked to those IDs. Today that number is around 38 percent.

Q: Private providers say specifications keep changing. What are you doing about it?

We have heard that feedback. From January, our state sandbox will offer a certification track with fixed release windows twice a year.

Q: How do you make consent work for patients with low literacy?

Consent must be meaningful. We are testing a voice-based consent flow for patients who cannot read the screen.

Q: What does success look like?

The goal is simple: no patient should have to carry a plastic bag of old prescriptions to a new doctor.

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Panel Discussion · Agri-Stack

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Putting the Farmer at the Centre of the Data

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Land records, offline-first apps and village entrepreneurs are making agri-stack real — but inclusion has to be measured

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Gurpreet Sandhu, Commissioner, Agriculture & Farmers Welfare

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“For farmers, the value shows up when a loan or an insurance claim gets processed without a middleman.”

— Dr. Sneha Patil

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Agri-stack is about putting the farmer at the centre of the data, not the scheme, said Manish Dubey of the Common Services Network, opening a panel that kept returning to the realities of the last mile.

Gurpreet Sandhu, Commissioner for Agriculture & Farmers Welfare, reported that land records have been digitised for 96 percent of villages in the state. The next step is linking them to crop surveys conducted by field staff on a mobile app.

Dr. Sneha Patil, founder of KisanGrid, said that is the real test of the stack. Advisory services in local languages are where AI can help, she added, but the advice must be accountable to an agronomist.

## Designing for no signal

Connectivity remains the bottleneck. Aparna Iyengar of the Rural Connectivity Foundation described field staff in some blocks uploading survey data at the end of the day from the one spot with a signal. Sandhu said offline-first apps were the single biggest improvement the state made: data syncs whenever the network returns.

Dubey credited common service centres for processing crop-insurance enrolments for farmers who had never used a smartphone. The village entrepreneur, he said, is the bridge.

Iyengar closed with a pointed reminder that women farmers are under-represented in land records.

> “Inclusion has to be measured, not assumed.” — Aparna Iyengar

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Technology

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: What “AI-Ready Data” Actually Means for Government

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Data inventories, named stewards and language benchmarks: the unglamorous groundwork behind every successful model

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By eGov Research Desk

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Prakash Nair, CTO, Kaveri Systems

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“The model was 91 percent accurate in testing. In the first month of production it dropped to 78 percent”

— Prakash Nair

elements.name: Body text (3 col)
elements.text:
^ Across the summit's AI, health and cyber sessions, speakers kept arriving at the same conclusion from different directions: the model is rarely the hard part.

The National AI Programme Office now asks departments for two things before it funds a model: a data inventory and a named data steward. The requirement follows its review of pilots, in which nine out of eleven departments lacked a clean, labelled dataset at the outset.

## Drift is the default

A model that performs well in testing can degrade quickly in production. Kaveri Systems described a grievance classifier that fell from 91 percent accuracy in testing to 78 percent in its first month live, because real complaints were written differently from the training data. Continuous evaluation, the panel argued, must be written into contracts.

Health systems face the same issue at the point of entry. If a diagnosis is entered as free text in three different spellings, no analytics system will save you, Dr. Arvind Kulkarni told the digital health panel.

## Benchmarks by language

Voice interfaces in local languages were widely seen as the largest inclusion opportunity. But accuracy is uneven, and panellists called for evaluation benchmarks to be published by language so departments know where a system is reliable and where it is not.

## A practical checklist

• A data inventory and a named steward before model funding.

• Contracts that pay for evaluation after deployment, not only delivery.

• Human review for any decision that affects entitlements.

• Published accuracy benchmarks for each supported language.

elements.name: Kicker
elements.text: Government Perspective

elements.name: Headline
elements.text: Redesign First, Digitise Second

elements.name: Standfirst
elements.text: Sunita Deshmukh on moving 212 services online — and why some of them struggled

elements.name: Byline
elements.text: By Kavya Iyer

elements.name: Caption
elements.text: Speaker close-up — Inaugural Session

elements.name: Body text (2 col)
elements.text:
^ A state mission director's account of what separates digital services citizens trust from those they merely tolerate.

Sunita Deshmukh's state moved 212 services online in the last three years. The ones that succeeded, the Mission Director told the inaugural session, had one thing in common: the process was redesigned before it was digitised. The ones that struggled were those where a paper form was simply converted into a web form — and citizens could tell the difference immediately.

The results show up in delivery times. The average time to deliver a caste or income certificate came down from 21 days to 4 days. But the bigger change, she said, was predictability: citizens now receive an SMS with a committed date, and the department holds itself to it.

Her advice on capability was equally direct. The best investment the state made was training its own district officers. Technology vendors come and go, she said; institutional capability stays.

elements.name: Pull quote
elements.text:
“we redesigned the process before we digitised it.”

— Sunita Deshmukh

elements.text:
^ The summit closed with the eGovernance Excellence Awards 2026. Host Siddharth Rao announced that the jury had reviewed 286 nominations from 27 states and union territories.

Jury chair Dr. Hemant Kulshreshtha said the jury looked for three things: measurable citizen impact, the ability to scale, and honesty about what did not work. Several entries came from district administrations, which he said shows that innovation is no longer only a capital-city story.

> “Most good ideas in government die because nobody wants to be the first to try.” — Rekha Pillai

Rekha Pillai, Additional Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms, said recognition matters because it gives officers permission to take risks.

The award for Citizen Service Delivery went to a district team that cut pension processing time from forty-five days to seven.

Pillai closed with a request to every officer in the hall: document what you did, so that someone in another state can copy it next year.
